She went instead to the shelf where the hinges were kept, and touched the edge of it as if checking for dust, and found none because he had been at it since morning. He stayed where he was with the broom in his two hands like a man at a gate.

"Halloran was in," he said.

"I saw him on the road."

"He wanted washers."

"He always wants washers." She said it without any humour in it, and yet it was a kind of joke between them, the oldest kind, the kind that had stopped being funny and become instead a place to stand.

The card had her mother's hand on it. He had known that before he turned it face down on the counter at half past nine, and known it again when he turned it back up at ten, and he had not read it either time. That was the decision. It was hers to open, or hers to leave, and he would not be the one to make the choice smaller by making it first.

She crossed the floor at last. The boards spoke under her the way they had spoken under her for thirty years, the third one and the seventh. She stood over the card and did not lift it.

"You could have read it," she said.

"I could."

"You didn't."

"No."

She put her hand flat over it, the way Halloran had spread his, and left it there, and the light went on shifting across the floor toward the door, and neither of them moved to stop it."}
